data.title: Chromoblastomycosis — viva
data.summary: Fungal infections · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Chromoblastomycosis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is chromoblastomycosis?**
- Chronic, slowly progressive implantation mycosis of skin and subcutis caused by dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi, producing verrucous plaques and nodules; tissue shows muriform cells

**Q2. Name the causative agents.**
- Fonsecaea pedrosoi (~90% worldwide; F. compacta now considered the same species), Cladophialophora carrionii (arid areas), Phialophora verrucosa, Rhinocladiella aquaspersa, Exophiala species
- India: Fonsecaea pedrosoi commonest — Western Ghats, Kerala, Karnataka, Sub-Himalayan region

**Q3. Who gets it?**
- Barefoot agricultural workers, men 30–60 years; implantation via wood splinters, thorns
- Lower limbs (foot, leg) commonest, then hands, buttocks

**Q4. Clinical types (Carrión classification).**
- Nodular, tumorous (cauliflower-like), verrucous (commonest), plaque (scaly, slightly raised), cicatricial (atrophic centre, spreading edge)
- Black dots on the surface (transepidermal elimination of fungus) — the best sites to sample
- Satellite lesions by autoinoculation and lymphatic spread

**Q5. What are muriform cells?**
- Thick-walled, dark-brown, round cells (4–12 µm) with septa in two planes — 'medlar bodies', 'sclerotic bodies', 'copper pennies'; the diagnostic tissue form
- Seen in KOH mount of black dots/crusts and in histology (even with H&E — pigmented)

**Q6. Histopathology?**
- Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with intraepidermal microabscesses, transepidermal elimination
- Mixed suppurative and tuberculoid granulomas with giant cells containing muriform cells

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- TBVC, lupus vulgaris (verrucous), sporotrichosis, mycetoma (no sinuses/grains here), blastomycosis, leishmaniasis, verrucous SCC, psoriasis, lichen planus hypertrophicus, podoconiosis/elephantiasis nostras, leprosy

**Q8. Complications?**
- Lymphoedema and elephantiasis of the limb, secondary bacterial infection, malodour, ankylosis, SCC in long-standing lesions; rarely haematogenous spread (brain — Cladophialophora bantiana)

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Small lesions: wide surgical excision, cryotherapy, heat, CO2 laser — combined with antifungal
- Itraconazole 200–400 mg/day for 6–12 months or longer (drug of choice); terbinafine 250–500 mg/day alternative; combinations (itraconazole + terbinafine, + flucytosine); posaconazole
- Cryotherapy to reduce lesions while on itraconazole; imiquimod as immune adjunct
- Cure criteria: clinical healing + negative mycology + histology

**Q10. Why is response poor?**
- Thick-walled muriform cells resist drugs, poor drug penetration in fibrotic tissue, chronic lesions are large at presentation

## Quick spotter facts
- Verrucous plaque on foot with black dots — chromoblastomycosis
- Muriform / copper-penny bodies
- Fonsecaea pedrosoi

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 19A (Chromoblastomycosis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
